basic_identification.name: Opt-out vs. opt-in consent infrastructure gap
basic_identification.originator: Identified by multiple actors: Spawning AI (Jordan Meyer, Holly Herndon, Mat Dryhurst), Concept Art Association, Ed Newton-Rex (Fairly Trained), artists and advocacy groups (including class action plaintiffs in Andersen v. Stability AI), EU policymakers (AI Act drafters), Karla Ortiz and other artist-activists. The gap is structural — no single originator, but multiple parties have articulated the problem from different angles.
basic_identification.geography: Global, with legislative focus in EU (AI Act), US (California AB 2013, proposed federal legislation), UK, and Japan. Artist advocacy concentrated in US and EU.

core_ideas.core_claim: Current consent infrastructure for AI training data is fundamentally structured as opt-out: artists' works are scraped and used by default, and they must actively register objections after the fact. This is structurally flawed because (1) artists cannot control data on third-party platforms that host copies of their work, (2) opt-out cannot retroactively remove influence from already-trained models, (3) the burden falls on individual creators rather than data users, and (4) no universal opt-out registry exists that all AI companies honor. No opt-in default exists where AI training requires explicit prior permission. This gap represents a fundamental infrastructure failure in digital art's relationship to generative AI.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Entirely specific to digital art and digital content more broadly. The consent problem exists because digital works can be scraped at scale from the web. Physical artworks in galleries are not scraped into training datasets. The consent gap is a direct consequence of digital art's native environment (the internet) being structurally exploitable by large-scale data collection. The problem scales with the quantity of digital art online and the capability of AI systems.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: The consent gap is a direct product of the attention economy's data extraction logic. Platforms that host art (Instagram, DeviantArt, ArtStation, personal websites) were built for attention distribution. AI companies exploited the same open-access architecture that attention platforms depend on. The attention economy trained artists to post work publicly for visibility; AI training exploited this visibility. The consent gap exists precisely because the attention economy's incentive structure (visibility = value) conflicts with the data economy's extraction logic (visibility = training data).
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: The consent gap represents a structural failure of intention. Artists intend to share work for human viewing and appreciation; AI companies use it for model training — a purpose neither intended nor consented to. Opt-out infrastructure attempts to retrofit intention onto a system built without it. Opt-in infrastructure would align data use with creator intention by default, but no such infrastructure exists at scale. The gap is between intended and actual data use.

market_economics.revenue_model: The gap itself has no revenue model — it is a structural absence. The economics of the gap: AI companies save billions by using scraped data rather than licensing from artists. Artists bear the cost (unconsented use, style mimicry, market displacement) without compensation. Emerging infrastructure attempting to bridge the gap includes Spawning's Source.Plus (ethical data marketplace) and Fairly Trained (certification for licensed training data). These represent nascent revenue models for consent infrastructure.
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure gap. The absence sits between content creation platforms, AI model trainers, and artist consent. It is a missing layer in the digital art technology stack.
market_economics.price_range: N/A. The gap is not a market entity. The economic value of the gap is measurable in terms of uncaptured licensing revenue: estimates suggest billions in unpaid training data value. [uncertain]
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: The gap is widening. AI training data demands are growing exponentially while consent infrastructure develops linearly. Each new multimodal model (GPT-4V, Gemini, Claude with vision) requires more visual training data. Opt-out registries (Spawning) process billions of images but coverage remains incomplete. No opt-in system has achieved scale. Legislative responses (EU AI Act, California AB 2013) are slow relative to technology deployment. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: N/A. This is not a market for collectors. The affected population is digital artists globally, estimated at millions of creators whose work is online and potentially included in training datasets.
market_economics.sustainability: The gap is self-perpetuating under current conditions. Without regulatory mandates for opt-in consent, the opt-out model persists because it serves the economic interests of AI companies (free training data). Sustainability of the gap depends on regulatory, legal, and market forces: if the EU AI Act's transparency requirements, ongoing lawsuits (Getty v. Stability AI, Andersen v. Stability AI), or market demand for ethically sourced data shift the balance, opt-in may become viable. Otherwise, the gap persists indefinitely.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Opt-out tools: Spawning's Have I Been Trained (search), Do Not Train registry, robots.txt and ai.txt directives, Glaze (style protection tool from University of Chicago), Nightshade (data poisoning tool). None of these are opt-in infrastructure. They are reactive defenses rather than proactive consent systems. The toolchain for opt-in consent does not exist at scale — Source.Plus and Fairly Trained certification are early attempts.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: The gap IS about AI. It defines the structural relationship between digital art practice and generative AI development. The consent gap means that AI models are trained on art without permission, can replicate artistic styles without attribution, and compete with artists commercially using their own creative labor. The relationship is simultaneously parasitic (AI depends on artist labor) and adversarial (artists resist unconsented use).
practice_aesthetics.liveness: The gap is dynamic and evolving. New AI models, new scraping techniques, and new opt-out tools create a continuously shifting landscape. The gap is not a static problem but an active arms race between data extraction and consent enforcement.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: The gap has generated distinctive vocabulary: 'opt-out,' 'opt-in,' 'do-not-train,' 'style protection,' 'data poisoning,' 'consent layer,' 'ethical sourcing,' 'fair training,' 'data laundering.' This vocabulary bridges legal, technical, and artistic discourse. The vocabulary is contested: 'opt-out' implies a right to refuse that may not be technically enforceable; 'fair training' implies a standard that does not yet exist.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: The gap itself represents enclosure (AI companies enclosing creative labor as training data). Opt-in infrastructure would represent openness (artists choosing to share on their terms). The gap positions the field toward capture (value extracted from artists without consent or compensation). Addressing the gap would shift toward commons (shared consent infrastructure benefiting all parties).

infrastructure_governance.openness: The gap is partially an openness problem: artists post work openly for human audiences, and this openness is exploited by AI scrapers. Closing the gap requires either restricting openness (paywalls, watermarks, opt-out tools) or building new infrastructure that preserves openness for humans while controlling access for machines. Spawning's Do Not Train registry is an open standard; Source.Plus is proprietary.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: No governance exists for the gap itself. The consent question is governed by a patchwork of copyright law, platform terms of service, voluntary AI company policies, and emerging regulation. No single authority governs the relationship between artists and AI trainers. The EU AI Act creates the most comprehensive governance framework but enforcement mechanisms are still developing (2025-2027 implementation).
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: The gap represents a massive data sovereignty failure. Artists have no effective sovereignty over how their published work is used for AI training. Even when artists opt out via Spawning's registry, compliance by AI companies is voluntary. The fundamental sovereignty problem: once an image is on the internet, the artist loses practical control over its use in training datasets. Retroactive control (opt-out) is technologically insufficient; only prospective control (opt-in) would provide genuine sovereignty.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Very low. No universal consent standard exists that is interoperable across all AI companies, platforms, and jurisdictions. Spawning's Do Not Train registry, robots.txt, and platform-specific opt-out mechanisms are fragmented and incompatible. The C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) standard includes some consent metadata capabilities but is not widely adopted for consent purposes. A machine-readable, universally honored consent standard does not exist.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Not directly a preservation issue. However, the consent gap intersects with preservation: if artists withdraw work from the internet to avoid AI scraping, that work becomes less accessible and harder to preserve. The defensive response to the consent gap (removing work, restricting access) can create preservation problems.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: This IS the consent architecture gap. Current state: (1) No universal opt-in system exists. (2) Opt-out is fragmented across Spawning (Do Not Train registry), platform-specific toggles (DeviantArt, ArtStation), and file-level metadata. (3) Compliance is voluntary for AI companies. (4) robots.txt is advisory, not binding. (5) No technical mechanism prevents scraping by non-compliant actors. (6) GDPR requires active consent for personal data processing but its application to creative works in training datasets is contested. (7) The EU AI Act Article 53 requires transparency about training data but does not mandate opt-in consent.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: The traditional art world is largely insulated from this gap because physical artworks are not scraped into training datasets. However, images of traditional artworks published online are scraped. The gap affects any artist whose work exists in digital form on the internet, bridging traditional and digital art worlds. Major art institutions have not taken strong positions on the consent infrastructure question, focusing instead on AI art exhibition rather than AI training data ethics.
field_position.what_it_enables: The gap enables AI companies to build powerful generative models using the creative labor of millions of artists without permission or payment. It enables style mimicry, commercial competition with human artists, and the commodification of artistic labor as data. Paradoxically, the gap also enables the AI art tools that some artists use creatively — the models could not exist without the scraped training data.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Everything. The gap IS the absence. Specifically missing: (1) Universal opt-in consent standard, (2) Machine-readable consent metadata interoperable across platforms and AI systems, (3) Compensation mechanisms for artists whose work trains models, (4) Retroactive remedy for already-trained models, (5) Technical enforcement (not just voluntary compliance), (6) Global coverage (consent standards that work across jurisdictions), (7) Identity verification for consent registrations, (8) Granular consent (allowing some uses while prohibiting others).
field_position.who_is_excluded: All artists whose work is online are affected. Most excluded from available protections: artists unaware of the issue, artists without English proficiency (most tools are English-language), artists in jurisdictions without relevant legislation, artists whose work was scraped from platforms they do not control (Pinterest pins, search engine caches, dataset aggregators), deceased artists whose estates are unaware, artists who cannot afford time to register opt-outs across multiple systems.
field_position.frontier_signal: Frontier. This is the most actively contested infrastructure gap in the digital art field. Legislative, legal, and technical responses are all in development but none has resolved the fundamental problem. The gap will either be closed by regulation (mandating opt-in), by market forces (demand for ethically trained models), or by technology (consent-aware training pipelines) — or it will persist as a permanent structural injustice.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Artist advocacy on social media (Twitter/X, Instagram), media coverage (New York Times, Wired, Ars Technica, MIT Technology Review), class action lawsuits (Andersen v. Stability AI, Getty v. Stability AI), legislative hearings, artist community platforms (Concept Art Association). The discourse was primarily driven by viral demonstrations of style mimicry in late 2022 and early 2023.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Moderate. The consent gap exists regardless of attention. But the political will to address it depends on sustained public attention to the issue. Artist advocacy campaigns require attention-economy amplification to influence regulation. The risk is attention fatigue: if the public stops caring about AI training data, legislative momentum may stall.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Strongly intention-aligned. Addressing the consent gap serves the declared structural needs of artists and the field. The gap represents a failure of intention: the system operates against what artists intend for their work. Closing the gap would bring data use into alignment with creator intention.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Addressing the gap would be a massive commons contribution: universal consent infrastructure would benefit all creators. The gap itself is a commons failure: creative labor is extracted as a private resource rather than managed as a shared commons with artist agency. Spawning's open opt-out tools contribute to the commons; Source.Plus marketplace introduces market logic.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Usage provenance — tracking how creative work is used (in AI training) rather than who owns it. This is a novel provenance category: not ownership or meaning but application. The gap means this provenance category effectively does not exist — there is no record of which works trained which models.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: The gap has an irreversible temporal dimension: once a model is trained on data, the influence cannot be retroactively removed (current unlearning techniques are inadequate). This means opt-out is temporally limited — it can only affect future training, not past training. Opt-in would be temporally correct (consent before use) but does not exist at scale.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: The gap IS an absence: the absence of consent infrastructure. It represents a structural void in the digital art field's governance layer. The gap forces the field to handle absence directly — confronting what does not exist rather than optimizing what does.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence. There is widespread coherence that the consent gap is a real problem. There is no consensus on the solution: some advocate for opt-in mandates, others for compensation models, others for collective licensing, others for expanded fair use, others for data poisoning as self-defense. The coherence-without-consensus dynamic is productive but has not yet produced a resolution.
coherence.contestability: Highly contested. AI companies contest that opt-in would be impractical or would stifle innovation. Artists contest that opt-out is inadequate. Legal scholars contest whether AI training constitutes fair use. Policymakers contest jurisdiction. The entire debate is actively contested across legal, technical, ethical, and political dimensions.
coherence.forkability: The problem definition is not forkable (the gap exists regardless of framing). Proposed solutions are forkable: any organization could build consent infrastructure, propose legislation, or create market-based alternatives. Multiple parallel efforts (Spawning, Fairly Trained, C2PA, legislative proposals) represent de facto forking of the solution space.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The consent gap as a first-order concern for A(DAI)'s infrastructure design. A(DAI) should build machine-readable consent into its own data practices from the beginning — not as an afterthought. A(DAI) should track the consent landscape as a critical field signal and map which platforms and tools have what consent capabilities. The granular consent models proposed by Spawning and others should inform A(DAI)'s own consent architecture.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The opt-out default. A(DAI) must refuse to presume that inclusion is acceptable without explicit consent. A(DAI) should also refuse the binary consent model (fully in or fully out) and build toward granular, context-specific consent. A(DAI) must refuse the argument that consent infrastructure is too expensive or impractical — the cost of not building it is structural injustice.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: A(DAI) builds knowledge infrastructure for the digital art field. The consent gap means that digital art is being used as raw material for AI systems without the knowledge or consent of its creators. A(DAI) must navigate this tension: building infrastructure that maps the field comprehensively while respecting the consent preferences of the practitioners it maps. A(DAI) cannot build consent infrastructure for AI training (that is Spawning's domain) but it can model what consent infrastructure should look like and track the gap's evolution.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: This is THE regulatory frontier. EU AI Act (2024, implementation through 2027): requires transparency about training data sources but does not mandate opt-in consent; Article 53 requires providers of general-purpose AI models to comply with EU copyright law including the text and data mining opt-out under the DSM Directive. California AB 2013 (2024): requires disclosure of training data sources. Proposed US federal legislation (AI TRAIN Act, various state bills): varied approaches to consent requirements. UK approach: initially proposed broad text and data mining exception, then pulled back under artist pressure. Japan: broad fair use exception for AI training. GDPR: requires consent for personal data processing but application to creative works is contested (Clearview AI precedent). Ongoing lawsuits (Getty, Andersen, Stability AI) will establish case law. [uncertain]
regulatory_legal.ip_model: The gap sits at the intersection of copyright law and AI policy. Copyright gives artists rights over reproduction and derivative works. AI companies argue fair use/text-and-data-mining exceptions. No jurisdiction has definitively resolved whether AI training constitutes copyright infringement. The IP model is in active litigation and legislative development.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: This IS the central question. Current default: opt-out (artists presumed included unless they actively object). EU DSM Directive Article 4: allows opt-out for text and data mining. GDPR: theoretically requires opt-in for personal data but application to creative works contested. No jurisdiction has mandated opt-in consent for AI training data at scale. The gap between opt-in aspiration and opt-out reality is the defining consent infrastructure failure.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: The gap depends on the entire internet ecosystem: web scraping infrastructure (Common Crawl, LAION), content hosting platforms (Instagram, DeviantArt, ArtStation, personal websites), AI model training infrastructure (cloud compute), and the absence of universal consent infrastructure connecting these layers.
ecosystem.network_effects: Negative network effects for artists: the more artists post online, the more training data is available without consent. Positive network effects for opt-out tools: the more artists opt out, the more comprehensive the registry becomes. But the network effects favor data extraction over consent because the extractors (AI companies) are fewer, better-resourced, and more coordinated than the millions of individual artists who would need to opt out.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Independent of NFT crash. The consent gap emerged from the AI training data controversy (2022-2023) and continues to widen as AI capabilities grow. The trajectory is: growing awareness (2022-2023), initial tool building (Spawning, Glaze, 2023), legislative response (EU AI Act 2024, AB 2013 2024), ongoing litigation (2023-2026), and still-widening gap between extraction capability and consent infrastructure.
